rv.q: Whatever it is, this Wuthering Heights casts its spell.
Her toolbox of fourth-wall-breaking japery, song, dance and puppetry serves her brilliantly well when adapting the right source material, and she is particularly excellent at detangling knotty plots.
The pair don’t quite make this strange, turbulent relationship sing, though; their love for one another – the kind of love that defies all logic and reason – is never fully convincing.
While it’s refreshing to enjoy and even laugh at such a dismal story, when the play does try to convey gravitas, the moment loses some of its credibility.
But while the interval break is positioned at a convenient time jump, there is so little event of consequence in the second half that the whole piece drags, rather slowly, to its conclusion.
Roughly two thirds is just the ticket for a cold February evening.
A strong cast does well with what they have been given, though sadly this rambling and unfocused production doesn’t hit the spot.
Every dramatic moment is treated as a zany joke — like a Spike Milligan sketch without any gags.
As a piece of theatre, Rice’s twisted vision of the Yorkshire Moors is transportive and engrossing for the entire three-hour running time.
Stunningly staged, aided by Vicki Mortimer's set and Simon Baker's sound and video, with top-notch performances, this production takes Brontë's classic to a whole new level.
If you’re prepared to share Emma Rice’s vision this is a compelling and adventurous piece of theatre.
The kinetic energy of the performances help the near three hours pass quickly.

cn.t: Emma Rice's anarchic adaptation divides critics with its wild theatrical flourishes—live music, dance, and bold staging earn praise for emotional power and stagecraft, but some find the spectacle overwhelming and the story lost beneath excessive embellishment.
